maintopic: POST-UNRRA RELIEF   EUROPEAN COUNTRIES-PROPOSED APPROPRIATION FOR 1947 NEEDS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: POST-UNRRA RELIEF   EUROPEAN COUNTRIES-PROPOSED APPROPRIATION FOR 1947 NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement on the present problem of post-UNRRA relief, in relation, more particularly to an appropriation for that purpose which the government proposes to recommend to parliament. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) has a statement which he desires to make respecting fisheries. It will
include mention of one of the methods suggested by Canada to provide a part of Canada's contribution to post-UNRRA relief. The minister's statement will follow immediately the statement I am now about to make.
As all hon. members are aware, one of the great problems of the post-war period has been the provision of food and other basic essentials of life to the devastated countries of Europe. It will be recalled that the question of post-UNRRA relief was urgently discussed by the united nations general assembly at its last session in New York. Because the programme of UNRRA was coming to an end before the real need of the peoples in war-devastated countries had been fully met, the general assembly recognized that certain countries must receive financial assistance in 1947 to avert hunger, privation and suffering.
Canada had played a leading role in relief operations both during and after the war, and the Canadian government was in strong support of continuing international action to meet-genuine relief needs. However, it became clear at the second part of the first session of the general assembly that a new approach to the problem would be necessary. To this end, the Canadian delegation introduced a proposal which was embodied in a resolution adopted by the assembly on December 11, 1946. This resolution established a special technical committee of experts, on which Canada was represented,, to study the minimum import requirements of needy countries. The committee thus constituted took into consideration the carry-over of relief goods from UNRRA into 1947 and estimated the probable receipts from exports from each country, together with resources which could be regarded as available from foreign loans and credits, shipping receipts, remittances and other sources of foreign currency. According to the committee's report, European countries which had been receiving relief required $583 million of financial assistance.
Intimately linked with this proposal was the question of providing to specially vulnerable groups, such as children and adolescents, in the war-devastated countries the food, clothing and other essential supplies which they require. To meet this requirement, a concrete united nations plan was agreed upon. The general assembly established by unanimous resolution the international childrens emergency fund. The prime purpose of the fund is to provide for children, adolescents and nursing mothers in countries which were victims of aggression, but it will also be used
Post-UNRRA Relief

for child health purposes generally. The fund has presented a tentative budget of $450 million, having as its principal objective one 700-calorie meal a day for twenty million children.
The funds is to be financed by any residual assets made available by UNRRA, by direct contributions from governments and by contributions from voluntary agencies or individuals. The amount of assistance available from UNRRA for this purpose is not likely to be large. Receiving countries might, however, contribute $200 million from their own resources. This would leave a balance of approximately $250 million to be secured from government and from voluntary contributions in other countries.
In the absence of relief on a scale at least approaching the sums recommended by the united nations technical committee, there will be serious hardship and possibly actual starvation in a number oif European countries this year, particularly in the period prior to the harvests in Europe this summer and autumn. In May 1047 the United States Congress authorized an appropriation of $350 million for relief purposes, to be dispensed by arrangements made directly with the needy countries and expressly limited to Austria, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Poland, China and the Free Territory of Trieste. This amount includes a sum of $40 million, all or part of which may go to the international children's emergency fund. We have been informed that other states have responded to this emergency by providing funds for relief.
In the light of the need which we believe exists, the action of other countries in that regard, and the availability of surplus food supplies in Canada, the government has decided to recommend to parliament an appropriation of $20 million for post-UNRRA relief needs in 1947. This sum which would be spent subject to such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, would include a contribution of approximately $5 million to the international children's emergency fund. The remainder of the sum would provide relief to certain specified countries, and would be administered by Canada in. consultation with other states which are adopting similar measures.

maintopic: PURCHASES OF FISH-PROCLAMATION OF FISHERIES PRICES SUPPORT ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: PURCHASES OF FISH-PROCLAMATION OF FISHERIES PRICES SUPPORT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some time the government of Canada has been giving careful consideration to the proclamation of the Fisheries Prices Support Act, 1944, and to the 
type of fish that the act should first apply to. This problem has been closely interwoven with what the government's policy on post-UNRRA relief would be, and also with the trade and tariff negotiations at present going on in Geneva. These negotiations have been and are being closely watched by the Department. of Fisheries, the deputy minister of fisheries having been present at Geneva during some of the negotiations on fish.
As the government's policy on post-UNRRA relief has just been announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I am now in a position to make a statement indicating the intention of the Canadian government on the matter of purchases of fish for relief for the 1947-48 production, and on the matter of proclaiming the Fisheries Prices Support Act, 1944.
As part of its contribution to international relief the government feels that it can make available out of Canada's production of fish during the present fiscal year, quantities of canned and salted fish of types suited to relief feeding. The types to be purchased will be dried salted cod, haddock, hake, pollock and cusk, pickled barrelled fish (herring, mackerel and alewives), bloaters, canned herring and canned mackerel and chicken haddie. In the case of salted fish which is produced mainly in eastern Canada, the commercial export markets are reasonably firm, but in frozen fish both the home and export markets are weak. It is the government's hope that the industry will divert as much raw codfish as possible to salting rather than to freezing. The government will be prepared to buy, at prices to be determined, up to 10,000,000 pounds of dried salted cod and related species, up to 40,000 barrels of pickled fish, up to
50.000	boxes of bloaters, up to 900,000 cases of west coast canned herring, and up to
100.000	cases of eastern canned fish, the latter being in addition to the current purchases being made in the east by UNRRA. It is hoped that quantities of cod and related species of fish can also be diverted from the frozen outlet into the canned form.
The details of the methods of purchase, of prices and other terms of contract cannot be announced until after discussion with the industry, and members of the industry are being invited to Ottawa to discuss this and related matters next week. The purchases however will likely be handled by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The prices to be paid for this fish by the government will not necessarily be at the levels at which UNRRA has purchased in the past season. Many raw fish prices have declined recently, and the increased volume of activity which

Post-L'NRRA Relief
these government purchases will provide to fishermen and operators should contribute to a lowering of costs. The government will, however, in establishing the prices give due attention to the raw fish prices being paid to fishermen. As I mentioned earlier, these operations are confined to the 1947-48 season, that is to the current fiscal year, and the government in no way commits itself to a continuation of relief purchases next fiscal year.
Of the $20 million just announced by the Prime Minister to be made available for post-UNRRA relief, up to $8,000,000 will be made available for fish purchases. This amount, it should be noted, will be confined to purchases of fish of the salted and canned varieties. For some time, however, the government has been endeavouring to find additional outlets for frozen fish in European markets, either through commercial channels or through relief purchases. Despite this attention no substantial market for frozen fish has been found in Europe. Exchange difficulties in some countries, lack of merchandising facilities for handling frozen fish in others, and expansion of Europe's own fish production have all militated against frozen fish exports. In the United States, the only remaining substantial export market, competition from expanded United States production and from the products of Newfoundland and Iceland have contributed to a lowering of prices, and have slowed down the rate of Canadian sales of frozen fish. In the circumstances the government believes that the solution to the frozen fish problem depends on increasing the consumption of frozen fillets in the domestic market. To effect such an expansion of our home market has its difficulties, but is a solution, as many hon. members pointed out in the recent debate on the fisheries research board bill, which would have a lasting benefit to the industry, and which should be physicall}' possible since Canadians consume only some 10,000,000 pounds of frozen fillets annually, or something like three-quarters of a pound per head. To take care of the frozen branch of the industry the government is prepared to proclaim immediately the Fisheries Prices Support Act 1944. Under that act a board will be established with five members and with advisory committees from the industry-both management and fishermen.
The act gives the board powers to buy and sell fish and to prescribe prices. The board will be established without delay. It will confine its operations during the present fiscal year to fish produced during the remainder of the 1947 season. It will be asked to prepare in collaboration with industry a
general distributional programme, including advertising, designed to increase domestic sales of fish of all species and kinds, and particularly packaged fish, and in particular to consider the specific species of the east, prairies and British Columbia in which the prices received by fishermen from the freezers are unduly low in 1947, and to devise means of maintaining these prices at or near their current levels. This programme of support will be related to the domestic market only. The government wishes it to be clearly understood that it is not prepared to support or subsidize the export trade in frozen fillets. The attention of the board, as I have just stated, is to be devoted mainly to the expansion of the domestic market. This expansion will be aligned to a new government programme of improving the quality, the grading of packaged fish, and the standards of inspection will be set up accordingly.
The prices support programme therefore for 1947 is aimed at expanding domestic consumption by improving quality and by giving close attention to the distribution costs of the industry which hitherto have tended to hold retail prices at levels that limited1 consumption. The programme of the board will be confined to the remainder of 1947 production. So far as fishermen are concerned, their current prices should be well maintained during the season, first by relief purchases of salted and canned fish, and second by the operations of the support board in maintaining fishermen's prices and in making additional sales of frozen fish on the domestic market.

subtopic: POWERS OP GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41

speechtext: Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the third reading of Bill No. 132, respecting article 41 of the charter of the united nations.

subtopic: POWERS OP GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not a copy of this bill. It is not in the distribution office or in the office of the clerk of the committee. I object to the way business is being done in the dying days of the session. When the business was announced on Monday night no reference was made to this bill, and I object to this bill being brought on at this time. The bill has not been printed in French.

Here we are considering something that will land Canada clean outside of the empire. Reference is made to the security council. In my opinion it is all council and no security whatever. We tried that in the old league of nations and you know' what happened. Now it is proposed on the ninety-seventh day of this session to turn over to the executive the functions and powers of this parliament to make treaties binding on this country and sign a lot of covenants anew. Why should we transfer to the executive these powers during the recess of parliament.
The minister referred this bill to the external affairs committee, and the committee met and whitewashed the whole thing. What countries have adopted article 41 of the united nations charter? The minister said that the foundations of the council have been soundly laid. It was mostly sound. They have not been laid at all. If this is the kind of security we are to have, it is no better than a second league of nations and we will get the same results.
I have never seen a copy of this bill. I have sent down to the distribution office three times for it.

subtopic: POWERS OP GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO ARTICLE 41
speechtext:
We tried depending on charters and peace pacts and notes in the old league of nations, but if you adopt the principle of charters you are inviting a third world war. The minister mentioned India as having adopted the charter. The government of India is only in the making. Britain gave India peace and justice and security for over a hundred years, what is going on there now? We have started the greatest civil war in history. The members of the British empire are our best friends, and unless we hang together we shall hang separately. None of them can go it alone.
The minister is a learned man, and he represented Canada faithfully and well at the united nations meeting. But the charter is a flat failure. Here we are at the ninety-seventh

United Nations
day of the session and not one hour has been devoted to the discussion of foreign affairs. I see my good friend the leader of the house is here today. I hope he will not allow a thing like this to go through. How many members have seen the bill? I have not seen it. I spent an hour trying to get a copy but I could not get one.
I am dealing with the charter of the UNO, March 1, 1947, the white paper I hold in my hand. How many hon. members have read it? How many hon. members know anything about it? I can tell the house that Australia will not sign article 41; they know something about it. There has been a lot of criticism of it. The UNO is a tower of Babel and a failure. The people are alarmed. We are transferring our powers and functions to make these treaties to our representatives, to the executive. the cabinet. I object to that principle. That is what led us into the first world war, and if we stick to this it will lead us into another war. The members of the empire are our best friends and dearest relations. They have always been our close friends. Instead of trying to keep the empire together we are disrupting it; we are allowing the UNO and the United States to scrap it. We are back to the old days of Geneva and security, and we all know what happened before. We all know what is going to happen because we are drifting into similar practices. The most notable effort made was made by the only real league of nations, the British empire. How does it come about that we are prepared to deal with every country of the seven seas but are not prepared to deal with the countries in our own empire? These are the people who stood by us in the past and will stand by us in the future.
The United States is a great country, and I am an admirer of it. They have representatives on the security council and you cannot blame them for that. As a writer in a great British paper said:
The most notable effort of the council so far. in my opinion is to divide the various parts of the empire one from the other. Ever since the United States of America left that great imperial group known as the British empire, because the British made it, the United States people have wanted to become a world power something like the one which they left. They want a new place in the sun.
They want a new imperialism. You cannot blame them for that. I do not blame them for it. We should be prepared to stand up for our country. We are going into a fools' paradise such as we had before, a second league, and making the same mistakes as the Geneva of old.
83166-291J
The United States have delegates there, and they talk about America first, last and all the time. The British delegates do not do that. Under the circumstances I think it is only proper that we should stick to the empire that we have had so long because they are the countries that have supported us. I would not call the government of India a government, and if we were told the truth we would all be of the same opinion. I tried to move the adjournment of the house to discuss these matters. This is the ninety-seventh day of the session and we have not had fifteen minutes devoted to this thing, the liquidation of the British empire. What are the conditions in India today? It is one of the countries that requested us to sign this agreement, to make a treaty out of it, to give the minister and the executive power over the head of parliament to bring us to the very verge of war. For 180 years India has been a great country and a great land. Under British rule India has had peace, security, liberty and justice for over 150 years. They have not much order there now. What would hon. members think of India if they could get a return giving actual information on the situation there today where there is civil war? Instead of tens of thousands there are hundreds of thousands being massacred in that land. We are proposing to give that country and its trade over to United States interests and to Russia. It will not be done with my vote. The outlook for the empire is too dark at present for me.
I wish to protest against this way of doing business. The Indian situation is a tragedy. The minister says that India has consented to this agreement, I would not call the government of that country a government. There are fifty million people there called untouchables who will be led like lambs to the slaughter. We do not know anything about it at all. It. is a serious tragedy. It is going to lead India to the greatest civil war in all history. Compared with what is going on in the Balkans it will be trivial.

Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this bill because in my judgment it is a bad bill and one which this house should reject. I believe as the days go by it will become more and more evident to the members of the house that they should not pass this bill. May I give some indication of the reasons I have for taking the stand I have indicated.
In the first place this bill binds Canada still more closely to the united nations organization. A great many people assume that there is nothing else for Canada to do than to follow along the line of accepting the united nations organization. My contention is that we made a grave blunder in this house when we accepted it in the beginning, and for us to go forward adding more strands, we will say, to the bonds which attach us to the united nations organization, when it is becoming more and more evident that we made a mistake in the beginning, is in my judgment simply sending good money after bad.
United Nations

May I give the reasons for the stand I am taking? This bill, if put into effect, will place the average Canadian citizen in constant danger and dread of the most hideous autocracy the mind of man has ever conceived, namely, the united nations organization and its all-powerful executive arm, the security council. When in 1946 Canada accepted the united nations organization and the united nations charter, Canada became a signatory to what was in effect a blanket mortgage on a basis of goods and chattels. The Bretton Woods agreement and the united nations organization charter were simply gold bricks as well as booby traps. The members who went from Canada to represent this country at the Bretton Woods conference and the San Francisco conference fell far short of what in my judgment Canada had a right to expect of them. Parliament has already taken several footsteps into the morass, the bog, the quagmire of international entanglements involved in the united nations organization. Surely we can sense the danger which threatens us. Let us refuse to accept this bill just now. Let us cautiously withdraw to solid ground, at least ground less treacherous than that upon which we now stand. Let us there circumspectly review the situation confronting us as Canadians. Let us reexamine every aspect, and let us reconsider our course of procedure. Every move we make now is fateful. Let us exercise	extraordinary

subtopic: INVESTIGATION. CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT- PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC

speechtext: Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 338, to provide for the investigation, conciliation and settlement of industrial disputes.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION. CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT- PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC
speechtext:
Before this bill is read the second time and referred to the committee on industrial relations, which is, I believe, the intention of the minister, I should Like to make a few comments. I shall have some criticism to make of the bill, and in an effort to avoid1 raising the ire of the minister I want to say at once that, all my comments will not be criticisms. The bill has its good points as well as its bad ones and I hope to refer briefly to both. I may say further for the minister's benefit that I realize as well as anyone can the difficulties, under a constitution such as ours, of drafting satisfactory legislation of this kind. In that regard the minister has my sympathy.
I would refer, first, to what I consider to be the favourable or good points in the legislation. In that respect I would say that the recognition of bargaining agents rather than bargaining representatives, as was the case with P.C. 1003, is a great improvement which,
I think, will meet with the approval of organized labour right across the country. Another good point in the measure before us is that it specifically provides that the Canada labour relations board which will be set up under this act shall consist of an equal number of representatives of employers and employees plus a chairman. I am sure that also will meet with the approval of labour organizations. Another good feature is the provision in subsection 8 of section 32 that- in proceedings before the board neither party can be represented by a lawyer or barrister or advocate without the consent of both parties, and1 even if the consent of both parties is given, the board may refuse to hear such representations. That is as it should be because conciliation boards are not legal proceedings, and every effort should be made to keep the proceedings under the board on a give and take basis of conciliation, free from technicalities and legal quibble. I commend the minister for putting in the bill the points I have mentioned. These three points do not, of course, exhaust the favourable features of the bill, but I wanted to refer to them first by way of appeasement. I am not ordinarily in favour of appeasing, but I thought it the best policy at this time.
To me, the fundamental fault in the bill is the restricted coverage. The provisions of the bill cover only a small fraction of Canadian wage-earners. Organized labour and others interested in legislation that would make for better employer-employee relations were hoping that when legislation for this purpose was drafted it would be much broader in scope than the measure before us. I am satisfied that in that way this measure is a disappointment to a great many. This bill can by no stretch of the imagination be called a labour code.
As I said before, I appreciate the difficulties that anyone attempting to formulate a labour code in this country would be up against, but that we have not something more comprehensive before us now is, in my opinion, due to the timidity of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). The house will remember that last year when the industrial relations committee made its report to the house the first recommendation in the report read:
(a) That the proposed dominion-provincial labour conference be called at the earliest possible moment to draft a labour code within the
Industrial Disputes

limits of the Canadian constitution and with a view to establishing machinery for the prevention of dislocations in industry.
That report was approved by this house, and I maintain that it constituted a direction to the minister from parliament to make every effort possible to draft such a measure as the committee had in mind. I do not think the Minister of Labour did all that could have been done to get the cooperation of the provinces for uniform labour legislation. I say that with all due recognition of the difficulties in the way. Of course I may be wrong, but I base this opinion on a statement made by the minister when moving the resolution on which this bill is founded, as reported on page 4230 of Hansard. He said:
Last year we had a conference with ministers of labour of the various provinces and their officials, at which we discussed the more important principles of a new federal law-and, I may add, in a very encouraging atmosphere of cooperation.
Now this is what I want hon. members to note:
The chief purpose of the conference, of course, was to obtain the views of the provinces as to when it would be most appropriate to restore to the provinces full responsibility for dealing with industrial disputes in industries ordinarily under their jurisdiction.
I was under the impression that the chief purpose of the dominion-provincial labour conference was to try to find a basis for national labour legislation. I do not think it was for the purpose of finding when it would be appropriate for the provinces to have restored to them the jurisdiction they held before labour relations were governed by the various orders in council passed under the War Measures Act. That would come, as a matter of course, when these orders in council or any legislation founded upon them expired. So that I think in that regard the minister has not done as much as he could have done, and the result is that this legislation and the provincial labour acts that were drafted during the last year do not provide uniform labour laws throughout Canada. Instead of having uniform legislation, we have nine or ten different acts relating to employer-employee relations, nearly every one of which is different from the other. If the Minister of Labour wants to achieve as large a measure of uniformity in legislation of this kind as I think his understanding of what is required d'emands, the arrangements made with the provinces in section 62 of this measure are altogether inadequate. Of the various provincial labour acts that have recently been enacted, in only one province, Nova Scotia, is the legislation substantially uniform with this measure. If 
we take the labour laws in the other provinces one by one we find that they have very little in common with this bill. The new act in British Columbia has some provisions similar to those in this measure, but taking it as a whole there are important differences. In Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec the labour legislation has little if any resemblance to this bill. In Manitoba. Ontario and New Brunswick the labour legislation is much along the lines of P.C. 1003, but again totally different from this bill.
The difference between the legislation in the provinces and this measure seems to me strange, if the provinces had before them the views of the Minister of Labour. Surely if the provinces had in their possession a draft of this bill before they drew up their own legislation they would have made some effort to bring their labour laws into closer relationship with the federal labour law. Either that or we must assume that the provinces are not interested in uniformity of labour legislation. In my opinion such uniformity is essential if we are to promote unity throughout this country. The conclusion I must come to, then, is that the minister did not impress upon the provincial departments of labour the desirability of labour laws such as recommended by the industrial relations committee and by this house.
There are in the bill two bad features I should like to mention. I may mention more than two, but I believe at least two merit special mention. The first is section 9(3)(a), which provides that there may be more than one bargaining agency in an industry. If that provision is maintained in the legislation when it is finally passed I believe the effect will be to make industry-wide collective bargaining more difficult, and it will also tend to create divisions and jurisdictional disputes in industry.

I understand its purpose, but in these days of mass production, when the craft is losing a great deal of the value it once had, I think the provision in the bill is bad. I would take as an example the trade union in which I still have membership, the street railway men. For all practical purposes that is an industrial organization, though it is affiliated to the American Federation of Labor, which is supposed to be based on crafts. It brings in carpenters, blacksmiths, machinists, and all the different trades necessary in that industry. I know that over a period of the years craft unions

have endeavoured to take these workers out of the amalgamated association and get them into the craft unions.

Where the principle is
already recognized, as it is in connection with the railroads, where the workers for years have been organized in their different trades or crafts, this provision would not be necessary in order to maintain the present situation, because it would be maintained in that industry regardless, I think. I just wanted to draw' that matter to the attention of the minister. Before he interrupted me-

speechtext:
I am sorry; I should
not have interrupted.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION. CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT- PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC
speechtext:
That is quite all right. I was pointing out that in my own trade union, attempts had been made to take out those belonging to the various crafts, but good judgment has always prevailed and for a period of nearly fifty years they have been covered by one agreement.
The second bad feature I want to mention is the length of time involved in conciliation procedure, even before a strike vote can be taken. I have calculated, I think correctly, the number of days provided in the bill; and it takes approximately ninety days, even if each step follows the other without any delay at all, from the time proceedings are started until a strike vote can be taken. I am sure the minister, with his experience, realizes the importance of dispatch in dealing with labour disputes.
There is in the bill another defect, what seems to me a departure from ordinary procedure, in that police court proceedings are to be applied instead of civil action by one party or the other, as I think has almost always been the case. The Ontario rights of labour act and the Saskatchewan act provide generally that:	(a) a union and its
acts shall not be deemed to be unlawful simply because one or more of its objects is in restraint of trade; (b) any act done by two or more members of a union, if done in connection with a trade dispute, shall not be actionable unless it would have been actionable if done without any agreement or combination; (c) a union shall not be made a party to any court action unless it could have been so made a party irrespective of the provisions of the collective bargaining legislation; (d) a collective agreement shall not be made the subject of any court action unless it could have been so made irrespective of the provisions of the collective bargaining legislation. I believe that is a definite defect in the present legislation.
There are several other points which I should like to discuss at some length; but, since the measure is to go to the industrial relations committee, before which witnesses can be called, and representatives from employers, organized labour and other interested parties may have their say, I am not going to take up the time of the house any longer.
In conclusion, let me say to the minister that I am in whole-hearted agreement with the words he used in concluding his speech the other day, when he pointed out that harmonious relations cannot be brought about in industry solely by legislation. Legislation can set the rules; and a provision can be made to make each party abide by those rules. That, of course, is as it should be. But before we can have harmony in industry, several things will have to be done. Employers will have to realize that, while they may own and operate the industry, it is really the use the people of the community or the country make of that industry which gives it its value. Consequently the community has a stake in the industry outside altogether the stake the owners may have in it.
Then again the employee must realize that the community has a stake in industry, and that when production is retarded or stopped the community suffers. So I say there are two important points which both sides will have to accept. They must respect each other's rights in their dealings with one another. Second, they must accept their social responsibilities to the community.
Industrial Disputes

With respect to organized labour, I wish to leave one or two facts with the house; anyone may verify these for himself by reading a little industrial history. Organized labour as we know it today came into being after the industrial revolution. For many years, indeed for nearly a century after that revolution, labour had no protection whatsoever from the state. As a matter of fact acts of parliament were passed to prevent labour from organizing to protect itself. So it is clear that labour organization had its birth in struggle and conflict, and it will take years of attempts at understanding and fair dealing before we can eradicate the evil results of the behaviour of employers toward their employees.
I am glad, and in my view the house and country should be glad, that in formulating this legislation, with all its shortcomings, the government did not adopt in its legislation the punitive provisions in the legislation which became law in the United States only yesterday. It augurs well for the future if we can resolve our difficulties on a basis of compromise and cooperation.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION. CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT- PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this legislation arises from the recommendation made last year by the industrial relations committee. It is an attempt to formulate a labour code for Canada.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION. CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT- PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC
speechtext: Why not call it an act?

subtopic: INVESTIGATION. CONCILIATION AND SETTLEMENT- PROVISION FOR BOARDS AND COMMISSIONS, ETC
speechtext:
The resolution asked for a labour code. The minister may call it an act, if he wishes. I said it was an attempt to form a code. The minister may quibble about the word used, and I am prepared to accept his quibbles. It makes no real difference what it is called.
The basic reason for the legislation is, so far as possible, to have a pattern for labour legislation across Canada. In this connection any action taken by the federal government must in some respects come into conflict with the British North America Act, which definitely prescribes that, with certain limitations, labour relations shall be in the provincial field.
Those hon. members and other people throughout Canada who believe that labour legislation is an open and shut matter should ponder section 92 (10) (c) of the British North America Act, which reads:
Such works or undertakings as although wholly situate within the province are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to 'be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
That, in my humble opinion, still gives residual power to the federal authorities. That 
is a part of the British North America Act which might be interpreted in the widest possible way.
In a country like Canada there is bound to -be difficulty in formulating uniform labour laws. The conditions of work, and the varied climate must be considered. Types of industry vary widely from one end of the country to the other. Such things, as hours and' conditions of work, wages and other questions should, in my opinion, remain matters to be dealt with by the; provincial authorities. Therefore I do not think the criticism that there is not a uniform labour law across Canada is well taken when all these difficulties are considered.
The first criticism I have to make is that this legislation should have been brought down a long time ago. The bill was initially circulated at the turn of the year and it was ready for presentation considerably over a month ago. It is an important piece of legislation and it should have been brought down for full discussion, in this house at that time. In view of the fact that we are in the dying days of the session and particularly when the country is being faced with induced difficulties caused by a major labour dispute taking place south of the border, it is perhaps unfortunate that this legislation has been so long delayed.
The test of all labour legislation is this: Will it promote industrial peace and maintain production? The fundamental fallacy of much labour legislation is that it is written against some body or is intended to be a curb on some activity or another. This legislation avoids many of the pitfalls we have seen in legislation elsewhere and as such it is to be commended. Labour law must not be punitive either way.
The first thing labour legislation should do is to protect the people of the country. The second thing it should do is to protect the individual freedom of the worker. During the past year there have been many instances in Canada where the individual freedom of the worker was not protected. Extremely arbitrary strike action was taken without the support of the vast majority of the workers concerned. As I say, labour legislation should take care to protect the rights of the individual worker. This bill is a short step in that direction.
We come now to one pofnt in the legislation which is somewhat of a departure from the old law, that is, that- conciliation proceedings must take place before strike action can be resorted to. That is one of the fundamental things that should be included in labour legislation; there should be an opportunity to talk the matter over before direct action is taken. To have left out that clause

Industrial Disputes
would have destroyed the whole framework of this bill. This is being resented strenuously in British Columbia. I realize that the case in question is a provincial matter; nevertheless there exists on Vancouver island a situation which is in direct defiance of bill 39 of the British Columbia statutes. I feel that this provision for conciliation is a necessary part of the bill.
The next point is the recognition of the responsibility of unions. This bill makes the union an entity. While I have no legal opinion on the matter, I understand that the union will be a legal entity before the board; that is, before the law. I think that is good; I think that is necessary. The union must accept the responsibilities entailed in acting as a bargaining agency.
The next point is that this legislation provides an opportunity for both sides to state their case. There has been a bad tendency not to allow management to state its case to the worker, but this bill contains a clause giving management an opportunity to state its case. That provision should be a necessary part of all labour legislation. Both sides should have equal opportunity to state their case. That is the fundamental law of democracy. The regulations covering that should be definitely and precisely stated.
We come now to the question of representation. I disagree with the clause in the bill which prohibits lawyers from acting on the board. I am not a lawyer; I am an engineer and, as an engineer, my outlook on problems is finite; there is a yes or no about it. A thing is so long; it is so strong; it has definite shape and qualities. In the training of an engineer there is little room for compromise; a thing, is either right or it is wrong. But when you are dealing with men, and frequently with angry men, there must be room for compromise and conciliation, and to disbar the legal profession from that type of work would be a retrogressive step in labour legislation.
Lawyers are trained as conciliators. We may object to them; we may have our views about the methods they employ, but conciliation is the essence of their training. To deny the one profession which has this training drilled into them through the years of university and law school is not assisting industrial peace across Canada.
In most disputes there is heat. People are very angry with each other. Management is angry with the union, and the union is angry with management. There is heat; there is hostility; there is even hatred. When you have management and union appointing someone who is not a trained conciliator, what is likely to happen? We saw it happen last year. The heat, the animosity, is, if anything, increased. Therefore I cannot agree with that section of the bill.
There are other things in the bill which, I suggest, can be better dealt with in committee. The definition of "employee" needs a great deal of clarification. I will mention just one point in that connection. One of the definitions of "employee" excludes from the bargaining agency employees who are in a confidential position with regard to labour relations only. There are a number of extremely confidentially employed persons who are not dealing solely with labour relations. I give, as an example, a man in a motor car factory who has the secrets of the design of next year s model, which is one of the most closely guarded trade secrets in all industry. I also suggest the technicians who are responsible for the control of alloys, or the composition of certain steels, and have a knowledge of special processes-all closely guarded trade secrets. I believe that such men too should be considered as confidential employees.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of all labour relations legislation is to bring about industrial peace and continuity of employment by which true security is obtained. This bill will be judged by how well it accomplishes this.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am very happy to be here this afternoon to say a word on this bill. I am one of those who in 1941 stood over in my place in yonder corner and commended the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the appointment which he had made of our present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). I have had something to do with teamwork in my short life, and the man who does not play with the team on which he is chosen is not much of a sport. When the minister took over this department I could not describe it better than by saying it was a hornet's nest. Labour from the Atlantic to the Pacific was burning hot. The leaders that he had to work with in his own department were, to put it mildly, not kindred spirits. They were not out to make his department a success so far as I could read into their findings. I am sorry that some of those leaders have not grown bigger and better. Some of them have.
One of the fine things that the minister did was the appointment of his present deputy minister. I took some pleasure in that, because he comes from that great city where the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) knows that men think for themselves, and when Mr. MacNamara was appointed deputy minister of
Industrial Disputes

labour, I began to see the clouds clear and that light was likely to come in.
The press has received the announcement of this bill favourably, and I have noted that two prominent labour unions have commended it. These same unions did not commend the minister in 1941. I was very glad that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), whose way of presenting things and whose honesty I admire, pointed out some of the good things in this bill. I think that was a splendid recommendation.
This bill has many new things in it and, on the whole, I think they are mostly good. They may not be agreed to by all the unions, but the legislation represents in large measure a revision of the wartime labour regulations with modifications and additions which are considered advisable following experience gained in their administration and in the light of representations received from provincial authorities and labour-employer organizations.
One of the line things the minister has been capable of doing is this. The word may not be quite suitable but at all events it is expressive, and that is that he is able to dicker with labour leaders. He knows their language; he knows their work; he knows their problems; he knows the difficulties they have in handling their membership. The minister himself has a long and honourable record as a labour leader, and I think labour all over Canada can commend the minister for this highlight in labour legislation. It would be interesting, I am sure, for someone to go over this bill and point out all the new things in it and show what benefits it will bring to employees and to employers as well.
My experience is that the man who toils must fight for everything he gets. The man who toils is never overpaid. He may get paid the standard wage, but my experience is that he never gets much more than he needs for his daily living. My experience of certain employers is that they are willing to cooperate all the way. I have known such men. One of them I worked with. He was willing to go all the way in helping his men to build up their homes, to improve their working conditions and increase their bank accounts. One of the things we have to do in the future is to give a little encouragement to the man who toils, because the toilers today need encouraging just as much as they did when they were far more underpaid than they are today.
There are one or two things in the bill which I think will prove very helpful. Employers are prohibited from interfering with or participating in the formation or administration of trade unions or of con-

tributing to their support or from discriminating in regard to employment of any person on account of membership in a trade union or because of union activities. That is a summary of section 4. This provision is similar to P.C. 1003 and is confined to craft groups. I do not think an employer has a right to interfere with a union. This bill provides splendid means to protect the employer and the employee. If they are enforced, then the employer will be happy and the employee will be contented.
As I said, the toiler has to struggle for everything that he gets; but my experience as a one-time president of a trade union is that not all men in a union are reasonable. The minister will know that. The president of a union has to be as patient as the minister; he has to keep these men in line so that they do not go over.
I was greatly impressed this year when one of the great things that visited the capital city was an organization that many cabinet ministers attended. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) like myself attended this meeting. It was a play put on in the Capitol theatre under the title of "The Forgotten Factor". Many of our ministers were there, and it was no discredit to see many hon. members from the opposition there on a Sunday afternoon watching the play. To me, that is the key to the solution of our labour troubles. You know as I do, and dear knows I love it much, that the love of money is a great curse. Whether that love of money is in the heart of the man who toils or in the heart of the man who wants to make big profits and dividends, it does not matter. The cure for our trouble today, both capital and labour, is that forgotten factor, men being

Industrial Disputes
willing to get down and discuss matters on a common foundation. That common foundation must be one which will not give way, and which is not built on sand.
The pictures that I have.seen of the report of that play indicated that it was put on by men from many parts of the world who had awakened to the reality that if you want to get the best out of a man you have to treat him with the Christian spirit. If you do that you will be able to meet him and be happy to see him, and1 you will be able to have refreshments of the right kind with him.
As I say, that foundation must be solid. To me, that foundation-and I am sure hon. members will pardon me for saying it, because I believe it-must be the love of Christ. When you build on that rock you will beat the devil to it whether he comes through money or in some other way.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, there will be ample opportunity for discussing the details of this bill, but if I have correctly interpreted one of the sections, there is lurking in it an objectionable principle, and it seems to me that this is the proper moment to direct it to the attention of the minister and of the government.
Under the heading of procedure it is stated that before a conciliation board the parties may be represented, but they have not an unlimited choice. The parties find themselves restricted as to the type of assistance they may retain to represent them before this conciliation board. Subsection 8 of section 32 indicates that lawyers, whether described as barristers, solicitors or advocates, may not appear before the board except with the consent of both parties. Even if both parties were to consent, it is still open to the board to deny such representation to either or both parties. It does not behoove me at this moment to enter into a lengthy discussion of this particular aspect of the bill. If there were brought before the house a bill in which it were said that a man suffering from a toothache might consult the grocer and the blacksmith, but might not go to the dentist; if it were said that a man much troubled in spirit might go to the theatre or to a concert but might not consult his pastor, and if it were said that a man suffering from appendicitis might see the tinsmith but could not go to the surgeon, we would think there was some peculiar aspect to the legislation and would wonder just why.
There is a profession which is neither young nor unknown that is peculiarly fitted by
training, aptitude and experience to represent other people.
The ordinary individual, not having given himself up to the studies that are necessary to the Marshalling and presenting of facts in all their ramifications, goes when he wishes his case to be fully presented to that profession which is learned in the statement of facts in their entirety. Just why it should have seemed proper to the draftsman of this legislation to exclude that body and deny the board such assistance as it could give is not entirely clear.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in discussing the present old age pensions legislation it must be apparent to all hon. members that the Liberal party-and I do not say this in any slighting way-has found itself hopelessly bound by an outmoded financial system. I think every member of that party recognizes, just as readily as we on this side of the house recognize, that the old age pension should have been almost twice what is provided in this bill; in fact I am of the opinion that if the members of the Liberal party were given a chance to record a straight vote in caucus, that is -where they would put the old age pension, at about S50 a month; and I doubt very much that any member of the Liberal party would favour the means test. I doubt very much that they would favour a good many of the other unhappy things involved in this bill.
I know the Conservative party desire a better bill; I know the C.C.F. party do also. Why are the Liberal party not giving us a better bill? Just because they do not know' where the money is coming from. They say they are in

the position of responsibility, and that must be granted. It is an easy matter for people outside looking in to tell how things ought to be done inside. It is a different matter entirely when one tries to tell what should be done, when he is inside.
I believe it is well to point out to the house that notwithstanding all their talk, if the Conservative party were in the position the Liberal party are in today they would not be doing one cent better. In fact I doubt very much if they would be doing as much, for the simple reason that you hear more talk about economy, as you heard more of that talk while the Conservatives were in power during the depression, coming from that party, without any clear idea as to where the economy is to be exercised, and how, than you hear from any other group of people in Canada.
Our C.C.F. friends have never made it entirely clear where they stand with respect to finances, but I gather that they would endeavour to raise the money through taxation also. If that is so I can tell you there would be a whole lot of extremely subdued members of the C.C.F. if they were in power in Canada today. They would be saying very little at . the present time, because they, too, would be faced with the problem of raising the money from the people. After all, if the money you can raise from the people is all the money you can have, and in a democracy that means all the people will allow you to raise, then what 3'ou can do for old age pensioners or for anyone else will be rigidly limited, as the C.C.F. would find out very quickly.
This bill, as it stands today, constitutes a condemnation of the financial policy under which it was drafted. Let no criticism be levelled at the minister. And I am not sure that very much criticism ought to be levelled at members of the administration. Once they agree, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) apparently agrees, that there is no way at all of getting money except by taxation, their hands are bound; bound by bonds they themselves have put on, but nevertheless bound.
A person would not be very far from the truth if he said this bill is designed and drafted under a system of "rob Peter to pay Paul". If you are going to rob Peter to get all the money you can pay Paul, then what you can pay Paul will depend upon how much you can take away from Peter. Perhaps that puts the matter about as simply as it can be put.
Although the words I am about to use may sound extreme, I believe very few members of the house and very few people throughout the country will wish to quarrel very energetically with me when I say that in effect

this bill has banished the senior citizens of Canada to a sort of Siberia of scarcity that it consigns the older citizens of Canada to a sort of restricted area of deprivation. I wish those words were really harsh, but I fear they are only too true.
I should like to put on record a quantity of information that has come into my hands since the beginning of 1947, which I believe people in future years will find interesting history, which people today can only regret, but which ought to fire people to far greater action than is in evidence at the present time. First, I should like to give hon. members and the people outside who read Hansard an excerpt or two from a letter coming from the old age pensioners' organization of British Columbia, signed by Mr. J. W. Hope. In this letter dated March 12, 1947, he uses these words:
The $10 cost of living bonus granted by the B.C. provincial government applies to the pension granted in this province, but not to the pensioners of other provinces, except in the case of Alberta and Saskatchewan, which did arrange for the interchange of the bonus of $5 and $3 respectively.
Therefore we have pensioners here getting $35 a month, others $30, others $28 and others $25.
As they are all in poverty conditions on such pensions, this discrimination, account of past residence, only makes their suffering more bitter.
The house will be interested to learn that early in the year, desiring to get some information right from the field, I wrote Mr. Hope asking him to have his investigators look up the cases of several people who were enduring life on the old age pension allowance. After he had conducted a sort of survey, he sent me this information in a letter dated February 20:
In response to our inquiry the following are the contents of the letters received from our members, showing the near destitution of the aged Canadian. This is the record and if you require the original letters I can send them to you.
(1) A. Wood, 2264 Triumph street, Vancouver, February 11, 1947:
"I am 72 years old, my wife is 67, so we have to live on our $30 a month for 'both. I prospected for 45 years, made quite a little money, and the same as all prospectors do, put it back into the ground. If it was not for the prospectors, there would not be the rich mines we have now. I helped to build the roads, bridges all over, to what are good sized towns today.
I applied for social assistance for help, but because I had a car I could not so turned it down as I have to take my wife in it as her legs are done. I went to work a little when I can, but my legs won't stand it any more, but I have to stick it so as to save my home by paying the taxes."

will do this man very little good. Thus from now on to the last breath this man draws he is literally banished to Siberian scarcity. He is confined to a restricted area of deprivation.

Then, here-is what Thomas Hepburn, of 5025 Union street, Vancouver, states on February 14, 1947:
I am at wits' end to know how to exist on the miserable pittance with the living costs increasing and coal up to $14.50 a ton. I cannot go to church as I have nothing to put on the plate. Cannot get clothes. Keeps me guessing to know what to do.
I will take one more. This is the letter of E. N. Veysey at 4411 Albert street, Vancouver, British Columbia. The letter is dated February 16, 1947 and states:
I cannot understand how the members of parliament can expect us to live on less than it costs them for cigars. However we are trying to exist. With coal $14.50 a ton. We can get no clothes. We are in bad straits. Cost of living increasing daily. So please do something.
I am going to read no more of those pathetic cases. There are some here which would almost make the angels weep. Here is the comment which Mr. Hope makes, after having given the list of ten letters:
Mr. Blackmore, I have seen some of these hovels, some unfit for habitation. These old people have to go the Vancouver Liberty to get warm. They are sick in body and spirit, how they continue to live and why is a mystery.
I believe that sort of evidence-and the rest of it is just as bad-is enough to show that I was not speaking unduly harshly or unduly severely when I said what I did regarding this new old age pensions bill.
Then, there are some most deplorable cases dealing with the incidence of the means test. I believe it would be only fair to those who would want to know the history of these times if they were told some of the things which have happened in connection with the means test. I shall take one example from Quebec and one from Alberta.
In a letter of April 25, 1947, from 487 Sanford avenue, St. Lambert, Quebec, Anna Hachey writes:
I am in hopes that it will eventually be decided in favour of the pension payments without a means test, because I know of at least one typical case where a man who is now over 80 years old and whose wife is 75 and an invalid, was recently refused his old age pension'for the reason that two years ago he was forced to make a transfer of his $2,000 savings to provide temporary lodging for himself and his wife. He now finds himself without any means of support, with no cash with which to secure clothing, medicine, etc., but the government cannot grant him his pension for another three years since apparently five years must elapse between the date of his transfer and his first pension payment.
What future generations will think of that kind of treatment of our senior citizens I tremble to reflect. I have a letter from

Alberta, from a man named Daniel Forbes who lives in Lethbridge. This is what he writes on March 6:
Enclosed find a letter received from the pension board at Edmonton as I have been making a few dollars to help me to have a comfortable living and the little I have made is none too much and the way the cost of living has gone up in the past six months if they are going to deduct that off my cheque I may as well not work for they are taking all I make.
Thanking you for the noble fight you are making for us to have the pension raised to a decent standard of living. Wish you the best of luck.
Yours truly,
Daniel Forbes.
And here is the letter dated February 25, 1947, he received from Edmonton:
Dear iSir:	According to the information on
our file you earned $295.54 during the year 1946. As this income is in excess of the amount permitted under the regulations our board regret that it is necessary to decrease your monthly old age pension to $10.78. You will however, still receive the provincial supplementary allowance of $5 per month, making a total pension of $15.78.
We are very sorry to have to decrease your old age pension but we trust you understand that the present regulations are very definite in the matter of income-, and the board has no choice but to comply with the regulations.
That is the kind of thing we are forced to by reason of the adherence to the present system of finance. It is not a question of how much milk, cream, butter, cheese, eggs and other kinds of food we have, how much clothing we can produce in Canada, or how much of anything else we can produce; it is a matter of how much money you can rob from Peter in order to pay Paul. If Peter has not enough money, then Paul has to go without, no matter how many goods the country is producing.
I wonder how many cases of this sort will be necessary in order to get into the minds of Conservatives and Liberals the fact that something ghastly must be wrong with a financial system which forces behaviour of that sort upon governments in this year of 1947. What is the matter that they cannot get to see that something is wrong? We have the people; we have the resources; we have everything in this country necessary to give everybody a high standard of living. Why are we not able to do it? How is it that the ordinary members do not ask themselves that question and demand of themselves that they find an answer? That is something which I must say I completely cannot understand. How it is that a member of this parliament, charged with the responsibility of conducting the affairs of this nation for four years, can disregard the potency of questions such as I have asked?

On previous occasions I have presented to the house evidence showing the incomes being received by the Canadian people. I have here a letter from the bureau of statistics, dated September 25, 1946, giving details of incomes earned by Canadians according to the census of 1941. One paragraph reads:
The percentage of wage-earners earning less than $450 for the twelve months period prior to date of the census, June 2, 1941, was 32-9 per cent; 28-7 per cent of the wage-earners reported earnings between $450 and $949; 29-9 per cent earned between $950 and $1,949 and 6-8 per cent earned $1,950 and over. 1-7 per cent of the wage-earners did not state the amount of earnings for the year.
How can people whose incomes are as small as those of the great majority of people indicated in that letter have a chance to help old people? What chance have they to save for their own advancing years? It is against that background that we must consider this
bill which provides only $30 a month for people who are seventy years old. All we need to do is to bear in mind one more fact, ' that it is almost impossible for anyone over fifty years of age to get anything like a satisfactory job in this country. Then we must realize that for twenty years-from the time a man or woman is fifty years old until he or she reaches seventy-he or she is faced with the awful prospect of being thrown into conditions such as are indicated by that report. It is simply bizarre; it is something which gets near to the point of being hideous.
There is a great deal more material which I should like to place on the record because I am sure hon. members would like to have it; but, after all, I do not propose to spend all my time tonight just talking destructively. All that I have said up to the present time has merely indicated the unsightly aspects of the picture. If I went into any considerable detail trying to explain how matters might be improved I would be called to order immediately, but I believe the Speaker will tolerate my reading a quotation from an eminent authority, the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, chairman of the Midland bank in England. The Right Hon. Mr. McKenna was so highly thought of in England that he figured prominently in the investigation of the Macmillan commission in Britain. His words are accepted as being of great worth. He presented a report to his shareholders which was printed in the London Times of January 30, 1936, so that it is pretty well up to date. He used these words:
Additional currency, however, can now he furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers, without reference to the central bank's holding of gold. Thus the nineteenth century, which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London, brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control.
Hon. members can find that passage in the London Times in the House of Commons library. If they go to Mr. Hamilton he will find it for them very quickly and they can read that statement. In the light of that statement, I am going to ask a question of three hon. gentlemen-I do not think they are all here now; I did not know whether they would be here or not; I shall not refer to them by name but one is a minister and the other two are private members on the Liberal side-who have spoken slightingly about social credit. They have been so sure that any departure from our present financial system would constitute rubber money or phony money.

I should like those three gentlemen, and any other hon. member who felt inclined to applaud them when in some cases they made their rather smart-aleck remarks, to read those words and do a little bit of good careful thinking. If those words are carefully observed and carefully reflected upon they will indicate a way out of the difficulty we are in.
It is the conviction of hon. members that conditions are painfully bad. Everyone in the house is ashamed of those conditions. Everyone is filled with regret, and no one more so than the minister, over the limitations which are obvious in this bill.
What are we going to do about it? Just talk and talk and talk while the time passes? That seems to be about all that some members think is necessary. I think myself that the time has come for us to do something effective about it. I would say that the Liberal party today, unless it is bound by some influence in New York or somewhere else, unless it is bound by some hidden hand in Canada, could do itself honour beyond anything it has ever done in its history if it would come out frankly and take that passage and say: If Mr. McKenna was wrong, someone prove he was wrong; if Mr. McKenna was right, somebody prove he is right; we are here to be shown, and until this gentleman is proved to be wrong, we are going to assume, having all the reputation that he has, that he is right; and we are going to direct our financial policy in this country in accordance with the principles he lays down in that passage.
If they would do that we should not have to have a ghastly thing like this bill come in next year. We should have something which would give us all gladness and let us all go out to the country full of confidence. We should have something that would meet Communism head on. Is it any wonder that communism thrives in surroundings such as are depicted by the letters from which I have read? Is it any wonder that the children of those people become reds? If we want to meet Communism-and I think every member of this house recognizes that Communism is probably the most dangerous threat to Canada at the present moment-we have to meet it with measures that are just as good as those of the communists. We have this advantage, that in this country we have one of the richest countries on earth. We have one of the finest sets of industrial development to be found in the world. We are fresh from a war in which we covered ourselves with glory by our achievements in production. We are operating under a system which can produce in super-
abundance. Surely if we make up our minds, we can produce so superbly that no other organization can possibly compare with us.
I propose to leave that aspect of the question and move an amendment to the bill. I have endeavoured, before moving this amendment, to express the opinion of a solution that I had in mind. Having done so, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low):
That Bill No. 339 be not now read the second time, but that the same be referred back to the government for their earnest consideration of the following provisions:
(a)	Reduction of the pensionable age to not more than 65 years.
(b)	Increase in the general pension to not less than $50 a month.
(c)	Complete abolition of the means test.

Since then we managed to balance our budget, and during the last fiscal year we had a substantial surplus, a surplus larger than all the surpluses taken together since confederation. For that reason I feel that we should be in a position to do a little better today then we were prepared to do in 1945. With the increased cost of living, $30 a month in 1945 is hardly less than $40 a month today, and it is very small.
A previous speaker referred to the fact that some old people have no relatives in a position to help them. I have knowledge of some elderly people in my own town. I know their sons and daughters, and they cannot look after their own families. How can they help their old people?

We must remember that when the Old Age Pensions Act was passed in 1927 it was intended to encourage the passage of social legislation by the provinces. The provinces did not want to go into the field, and for some years after 1927 the contribution by the federal government was fifty per cent. Then in 1931 the contribution by the federal government was increased to seventy-five per cent, and the four provinces which had not come into the scheme then came in. It is up to the provinces to see that their old people are properly looked after, and it is only just that they should be prepared to pay the same proportion as the federal government is paying and thus provide a pension of $45 a month for our old people.

If we want to follow the suggestion of the Union des Electeurs, represented by the hon. member for Pontiac, there would be 460.000 persons who are more than seventy years of age and who would1 be entitled, to receive a pension; then there would be 307,000 between the ages of sixty-five and sixty-nine years and 407,000 between the ages of sixty and sixty-four years. That would make a grand total of 1,174,966 persons receiving pensions without a means test. That is exactly one-tenth of the population. If each of those persons is to receive 860 a month it means a grand total of $845,975,520. The people would have to pay for that. If you added to that the $20 dividend which has been spoken about you have a grand total of over three and a half billion dollars a year. That is more than was spent during the war. The people would have to pay in taxation eight times the exemptions they were granted this year by the budget. Not only would they have to pay what they have been exempted, but the amount would be increased eight-fold. I do not- think the people of Canada are ready to accept anything of that sort.
I was surprised to hear that proposal made by the hon. member for Pontiac, a riding in the province of Quebec. I recall some years ago that a certain gentleman who apparently has certain authority in outside circles complained that Quebec was receiving more than its share of the baby bonus or family allowances. It turns out that in 1946 Quebec received $8,753,000 more than Ontario. I am not suggesting that it would be bad if the shoe were on the other foot, but the fact is that if we followed the suggestion of the hon. member for Pontiac, Quebec with only 104,000 old people would receive $75,000,000. whereas Ontario with 184,000 old people wrould receive $133,000,000. If the reasoning of the hon. gentleman is good, then I do not think the province of Quebec could be called upon to pay $57,000,000 a year for older persons in Ontario. I do not say it is good, but the argument is just as sound as that made by Mr. Drew some years ago.
If my hon. friends on the other side want to pay a pension of $50 a month; if the hon. member for Pontiac wants to pay a pension of $60 a month, there would be no difficulty about doing it on a contributory basis. There
is nothing to prevent the Dominion of Canada from paying three-eighths of the $60, which would be $22.50; the province could pay one-eighth, or $7.50, which is exactly what they are called upon to pay here, and there could be a contribution by the whole of Canada for the other half.
A contributory plan could be worked out whereby one-third would be paid by the dominion government, one-third by the province and one-third by the whole of Canada. Employers could be called upon to pay a certain amount and employees also. If each of the groups which I have mentioned paid an amount similar to that which will now be paid by the dominion government, $22.50, it would not be $60 that these older people would be receiving, it would, be $67.50.
I do not think it is fair to the population of Canada to burden them with taxes or to burden future generations by borrowing money. The federal government should not be asked to take out of its coffers at the present time the $875,000,000 which is asked for by the hon. member for Pontiac. People who are suggesting these large advances in the pension other than on a contributory basis are rendering a very poor service to our aged people. They are putting in their minds dreams that cannot be realized at the present time. That is a disservice they are rendering to these people, because they are making them unusually and unnecessarily unhappy.
The present bill contains a provision for a pension for the blind at the age of forty. Last year, according to the public accounts of 1946, 6,945 blind people received a total of $1,526,747 in pensions. If the age limit for the pension for the blind people were reduced from forty to twenty years it would add only 1,164 people, and at the current rate would mean an additional expenditure of $314,280- I did not say millions, but thousands. That is an amount that could be very easily absorbed in our budget. The blind must have been resident in Canada for twenty years to receive a pension, so that if they started to receive their pension at twenty years of age it would mean that they had been here and been blind practically from birth. It would be a great help to them to receive the pension at twenty.
I have nothing further to add, Mr. Speaker. Inasmuch as the old age pension is primarily a provincial matter and the federal government went into it only because the provinces did not want to act, I think the provinces should do as well as the federal government and pay $22.50 to each one of their pensioners, who thereby would receive a total of $45 a month.
