Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Restigouehe-Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) on the fine address he delivered tonight, and more particularly on his courage and sincerity in speaking out his mind as he did. I would point out that, unless * the old age pension is approached from the angle that he advocated and which the Social Credit members have advocated for many years, the problem will not be solved. I am glad that the Liberal party has two new monetary reformers in its ranks to take the place of the former member for Vancouver-Burrard, now Senator McGeer, and the former member for Parry Sound, (Mr. Slaght). If we may judge from their speeches these two new monetary reformers are the hon. member for Restigouehe-Madawaska and the hon. member for Fraser valley (Mr. Cruickshank). We welcome them, and I would suggest that they should begin to work on the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Rinfret). I think that would be a good beginning.
The problem of old age pensions, pensions for the blind, and pensions for the physically infirm who are incapable of supporting themselves is so important that I do not consider it necessary to apologize for taking part in this debate. The large majority of the members of this house will, I think, concede one point to the minister, and that is that the amending bill will improve the old act. On the other hand, I am of the opinion that the majority of members on both sides of the house were disappointed and shocked when they read the provisions of the bill, especially after the build-up and the promises which the government have made in the course of the past few years. I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is conscious of this fact without its being told to him. But in fairness to the minister I will give him credit for the few improvements made by this bill. I consider it proper that I should point out the defects which have not been removed from the old act and its shortcomings.
The most disappointing feature of this bill is that it does not lower the age at which assistance can be provided between the ages of sixty and seventy years to people who are in dire circumstances, with no means of livelihood, and who must depend on charity. The exclusion of this group from the benefits of thp act is cruel, inexcusable and unforgivable.
The large group of aged people who should have been taken into consideration are those between sixty and seventy years of age who have no means of livelihood. I have in my

hand a report of the old age pension board of Alberta, giving the numbers of those granted pensions in 1943. There were 769 who had reached the age of seventy, or 58 '65 per cent of the total number who qualified for old age pension; 145 received the pension at the age of seventy-one, or 11-06 of the total; 94 received the pension at the age of seventy-two, or 7-17 per cent; 69 received the pension at the age of seventy-three, or 5-26 per cent of the total; 52 received the pension at the age of seventy-four, or 3-93 per cent; 30 received1 the pension at the age of seventy-five, or 2-28 per cent; 92 received the pension who were from seventy-six to eighty years of age, or 7-01 per cent of the total; 56 were granted pension who were from eighty-one to eighty-nine years of age, or 4-27 per cent. Only four who were ninety years of age and upwards received the pension, and they constituted 0-3 per cent of the total. According to the Canada Year Book, there were 767,815 persons of sixt}r-five years of age and over in Canada in 1941. Those of seventy years of age and over numbered only 450,091 persons. These figures prove conclusively that the old age pension problem is not entirely in the group of those of seventy years of age and over but also of those of sixty years of age and over.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare gave sixteen methods by which the old age pension problem could be solved, and I wish to place these on record. Speaking in this house on June 18 on this very subject, the minister went on to point out the way in which the old age problem could be solved. I took the trouble to dissect from his speech these statements and I shall now put them on record. He said1, as reported on page 4285 of Hansard:
The measure which is being introduced today will make it possible for the provinces to increase by 20 per cent or more the assistance which has been given to date to this substantial section of our aged population. Where, because of outside income, pensioners have not been receiving the full pension, the increase which the provinces will be enabled to give under the new legislation will be even greater than 20 per cent.
The second suggestion for solution of the old age pension problem reads as follows. I quote from the words of the Minister of National Health and Welfare:
It is estimated that when the provinces have taken full advantage of the increases in maximum income allowable for aged and blind persons which are permitted by this proposed amending bill, the result will be an increase in the pension rolls of something between 60,000 and 65,000 additional persons.
There again, Mr. Speaker, you will note that the minister endeavoured to push the

Old Age Pensions
problem on to the provinces. I continue with solution No. 3:
If the provinces take full advantage of these new provisions, the provincial share of old age pensions under the act itself will advance from approximately sixteen million dollars to approximately twenty-three million dollars.
Solution No. 4:
It is proposed, in this amending hill, to do away with the provision which has been in the act up to the present time, section 9 (d), setting the maximum pension which any province is permitted to pay. Under these new amendments, therefore, the provinces themselves will be free to fix the maximum pension.
There again the minister endeavours to shift at least part of the weight of the problem of old age pensions upon the provinces. The fifth method for the solution of this problem reads as follows:
The practical effect of this will be that any province will be free, if it chooses to do so, to set a pension rate as high as $50 a month or $600 a year for a person who has no other income of his own with which to supplement his pension allotment.
Solution No. 6:
I have already stated that the department's estimate for this increase is about 60,000 additional pensioners, assuming of course that all the provinces will take full advantage of these higher income limits.
Solution No. 7:
In other words, a province will be assured that, on the basis of a pension of $30 a month, it will receive reimbursement from the federal treasury to the extent of seventy-five per cent Df its net payments. At the same time it will be free to provide pensions higher than $30 a month if it deems it advisable to do so.
I do not wish to weary the house with these quotations, but I believe that in arriving at an explanation we must consider the statements made by the minister in the course of one speech. Solution No. 8 reads as follows:
By removing the pension ceiling and by increasing the federal contribution the government is, in fact, opening the way for the provinces to pay more than $30 a month.
Solution No. 9:
No bill which this parliament can pass can in any way affect what a province may do within its own constitutional jurisdiction.
Solution No. 10:
In summary, it will be apparent that the result of the present amending bill will be in effect to set a standard minimum pension of $30 a month in all the provinces, assuming, of course, that all the provinces will be anxious to take full advantage of the federal contribution. More than this, however, it will undoubtedly result in a number, and perhaps even a majority, of the provinces of Canada going beyond this $30 pension to set higher pension rates in their respective provinces.
Solution No. 11:
Nothing in the federal Old Age Pensions Act as it will be amended by this present bill debars any of these provinces from incorporating their present provincial supplements into their basic pension rates, and it is thought that the provinces already paying provincial supplements will, in fact, be encouraged to maintain their provincial contributions on at least the present basis.
Solution No. 12:
What this bill will accomplish, if the provinces take full advantage of its provisions, may be summarized in this way:
1.	It does away with the provision limiting the maximum pension which any province is permitted to pay.
2.	It establishes a basic standard pension of $30 a month to which the dominion will contribute and leaves the provinces free to increase the standard pension rate as they deem advisable.
I have only four more references in this regard. Solution No. 13:
What we do now must be consistent both with present need and the need of tomorrow. It must be consistent with what we are trying to achieve with the joint cooperation of the provinces.
Solution No. 14:
The measure which is today being placed before hon. members of this house for consideration lias been deliberately designed to keep within the framework of the dominion's proposals to the provinces on assistance to the aged.
Solution No. 15:
The task of this government in cooperation with the provinces is to provide for the welfare of the nation as a whole.
Solution No. 16 and the last:
National programmes of such a broad and fundamental nature cannot be achieved in a country like Canada only by the central government. They can be achieved by all governments. dominion and provincial, acting in cooperation to ensure the greatest possible measure of well-being, economic security and social welfare for the Canadian people.
This present measure, representing as it does a joint cooperative effort of the dominion and the provinces, brings us one step nearer to the achievement of the objective that we seek.
Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out at the outset, my purpose in reading the statements which the minister made in the course of his speech was to show that the present position of the government is to shift a large part of this responsibility upon the provinces. Some of the ministers have gone so far as to say that it was the traditional policy of the government to recognize only a part of the responsibility for this problem and the provinces had to assume the rest.
I must congratulate the minister on his ability to put over his speech as well as he did. As a matter of fact, it did occur to me that had anyone else endeavoured to deliver the speech which the minister delivered the other
Old Age Pensions

day he simply could not have covered the inadequacies of the bill as well as the minister did. Not only that, but he was successful in getting the provincial premiers and legislatures to bite. The very next day or the day after, the premier of Ontario came through with a grant that made up the difference between what the federal government contributes and the provincial contribution to make a total of $40 a month. As I said, some of the provincial premiers and provincial governments considered that they were taking advantage of a situation and felt it would be a popular thing to do, so they went ahead and said, "We will pay a certain amount."
The other day the hon. member for Fraser Valley read part of the same quotation I intend to read. The former member for Vancouver-Burrard, Mr. McGeer, did place the same quotation on Hansard once before, but in this connection it is important to point out the position which the party now in power held on this question and the position to which they have lately shifted. Reading the debates in Hansard of June 2, 1931, I find at pages 2260 and 2261, the following words in a speech delivered by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King):
The Liberal administration fought for many years for an old age pension act, and care I think was taken to make it clear that an amendment to the British North America Act would be required before this federal government would have power to administer an old age pension scheme. It was recognized that an amendment to the British North America Act would take some time, and for that reason the government of the day adopted the method of agreeing to give these grants in aid to the provinces on condition that they would carry out a scheme framed by the federal government which would be similar in all the provinces.
An hon. Member:	A vicious principle.
Mr. Mackenzie King:	The principle, from a
financial point of view, was unsound. I am quite prepared to concede that. But I will go a step further and say that, in my opinion, this parliament ought to remedy the unsoundness of the principle, not by discontinuing to vote money for old age pensions, but by assuming the entire obligation, one hundred per cent. This government should take over the whole scheme and itself pay out the money. That is the position that should be taken; that is the proper way to remedy what there is of unsoundness in the principle.
Obviously the principle is thoroughly sound. I have always taken that position and have fought strenuously for it; and to get that principle recognized by parliament I was prepared to go so far as to support a grant in aid, which I am perfectly frank to admit was, from the point of view of financing, an unsound method. Now I say, let us recognize that the principle of old age pensions itself is perfectly sound and involves an obligation which the federal parliament should assume. Let us undertake to administer the Old Age Pensions Act from Ottawa
[Mr. Hlynka.l
and have all the moneys wdiieh are necessary for the payment of those pensions voted by this parliament.
Now I ask you, Mr. Speaker, does that not prove conclusively that the government at the present time has switched around in its position on this question? That is plain enough. I mentioned that there were six disappointing features in the bill, six extremely disappointing features, and when the minister speaks in closing the debate I should like him to tell the house and the country how he would propose that persons between the ages of sixty and seventy should live, persons who have no income, persons who have no means of earning a single dollar. How does he, being responsible for this legislation, propose that these people shall get along? What has the federal government in mind for these people? That is what I should like to know, and I am sure the country would like to know it as well.
The second disappointing feature of the bill is that it fails to provide any assistance whatsoever for persons who, for reasons of physical infirmity, cannot earn a livelihood, regardless of age. The total exclusion of this group from any benefits under this bill is also nothing short of cruelty.

I thank the minister for his kindness in this regard, because that is one serious problem which has so far been ignored. You see old men, crippled men, amputation cases, sitting on the sidewalks in every city of Canada begging. I think it is a disgrace to this country. Surely this government or any other government that is responsible for the care of these people should by now have granted some assistance to them so that they could live like human beings.
To go on from there, the third disappointing feature of the bill is that it does not lower the age qualification for blind persons to at least twenty-one and preferably to eighteen, when normally young people cease to depend upon their parents. The fourth disappointing feature is that the amending bill does not remove the means test, and finally the fifth criticism I offer is the serious shortcoming in the inadequate amount of the pension. Time will permit me to point out only a few of the more serious shortcomings, but I might say that, but for the minister's ability to cover up, by his oratory, the hopeless inadequacies of the bill, there would be sufficient reason for a nation-wide protest in connection with this legislation.
I had intended to place on record some of the resolutions which have been sent to us, and if time permits I may still do so. However I should like now to rush through a few of the suggestions I have jotted down. I must say that truly I did not expect a much better bill from the government at this time. In the past few years I have learned that these things are brought in ordinarily in such a way as to coincide with elections, and I realize that to grant all these benefits at this time would rather let people cool off by the time an election came along. So I quite appreciate that the government had to keep something in reserve for an eventuality which no doubt will come about. I do not blame them for it. They have made a great success; they have capitalized on this scheme, which has paid dividends to the party in power. But it seems to me that this question is too important to 83166-294
be used as bait in any election. It is a question which should be faced, regardless of where the member may sit in this house and regardless of his views. I believe this is one problem which must be approached from a humanitarian point of view. I regret that the minister's speech had a political tinge, as a result of which he brought upon himself a great deal of criticism which he could have avoided by refraining from his references to what the government did in 1927, and so on, though that is only a suggestion. I also realize that we are criticizing the wrong minister. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is absolutely innocent as far as any sins in connection with this problem are concerned. He is simply told by certain gentlemen, "You are going to have so much money at your disposal, and that is all." The poor minister has to make the best of it. It is a stop-gap, a bridge, if we may so express it, temporarily to take care of an emergency situation until necessary taxation agreements can be reached with the provinces. What could be plainer than that? I would not be on my feet supporting the present measure if this were the final measure to be introduced by the government in regard to old age pensions. I would be on my feet, just as my hon. friend was, bitterly denouncing the measure. But it is not a final plan; it is simply a temporary measure to grant urgent and needed relief for the time being until we can achieve what we are seeking.
Some other hon. members have been even more extreme than the hon. member who has just spoken. The present amendment has been dubbed "puny", "peanuts", "mouse" and the like. All these statements show clearly that at least seventy-five per cent of the critics of the bill do not know its provisions. They did not take the trouble to listen to the minister, or to read his speech, if they were not in the house when it was delivered.
In the first place, as honestly as I can and as fairly as I can I want to convey to the house what my folk back home are thinking about old age pensions. I find widespread feeling, a. positive demand, for social security. They want us to banish the fear that arises in men's minds as the result of old age, illness, unemployment and the like. They feel too that Canada is a wealthy country, that a country which made the magnificent contribution this country made in time of war can afford such a measure. They have no doubts on that subject.
There is another widespread feeling, just as prevalent as the one I have mentioned. They do not want charity; they do not want a dole; they want these things as a matter of right. They want to contribute to these different plans, to the health plan, to the old age pension plan and to the unemployment insurance plan. Canada did not reach her present, proud position among the nations of the world by anything but thrift and hard work and courage. Our people are self-reliant people. They do not want the dole; they do not want charity; they want these things as a math r of right, and they

want to pay for these pensions in advance during the years that they are working and able to pay for them.
Another thing; my folk back home do not like the tangle we are in today. They are very critical of it. They say to me, "It is our money you are spending; it is our money the provinces are spending, not your money." It is money that we take from the taxpayers that we are talking about, and they do not like the present tangle we are in. Anyone, whether it be the premier of a province, a member of this government or anyone else who holds up the procession will have to answer to the voters of this country in the long run. I find that folk are determined- that fear shall be banished from their lives, fear arising out of old age, ill health and the like.
I think we should take sufficient time to get all the different viewpoints and we should seek honestly for a solution. But in seeking for a solution I think the first thing we have to do is to face up to the facts even if some of them are unpleasant to me and to my hon. friends of the opposition. In the first place, I think we all agree that under our constitution nothing can be done in the way of a contributory health scheme or a contributory old age pension scheme without the concurrence of the provinces. I do not think anyone would dare to question that statement. That being so, the first thing we have to do is to reach an agreement with the provinces. That being so, let us have a look at some of the facts.
We all know that during the war the federal government, by -agreement with the provinces, was given the entire taxation field in regard to income taxes and- corporation taxes. The provinces vacated those field's. Why? Simply that we might make an all-out war effort. The scheme worked very well. No one was hurt. We came out of the war with the provinces all having surpluses. So I suggest that the provinces had no right to be suspicious of the proposals made to them, by the federal government at the time of the dominion-provincial conference.
Let us have a look at those proposals for a ninute. Here are the federal government proposals. They proposed a general over-all post-war scheme. First, there was a public investment policy, a policy under which millions of dollars would be spent at the right time for the welfare of our economy. Then they proposed under social security a national health programme and outlined that in detail. Then they proposed a national old age pensions scheme and outlined that in detail. Then they proposed further unemployment assistance. For the purposes of the debate tonight I am just going to elaborate the national old age pensions scheme.
Briefly, the scheme was that the provinces would vacate entirely the field-it is their field-that they would voluntarily vacate it and that the federal government would assume full responsibility for the payment of pensions to persons seventy years of age and over; that $30 a month would be paid without a means test.
Just here may I digress for a minute? I do not think many of the speeches in this house have struck at the core of the problem. While it may not be the most serious feature of old age pensions, I think the biggest part of the problem is created by folk who have worked hard and saved a little money, who have a little bank balance and perhaps own their own homes. They want a pension when they come to seventy years to supplement their own earnings and to make the declining years of their lives pleasant ones instead of years of poverty. That is perhaps the greatest part of the old age pensions problem, although perhaps not the most pressing. That problem has not been emphasized at all in the discussion tonight and I just wanted to call attention to it.

I am not arguing the case of Ontario and Quebec so far as their stand on financial arrangements is concerned, although I have previously said and still maintain that the correct method of getting agreements is, first, to discuss the objectives which we desire to accomplish and to agree on that. If you fail the first time come back again. Confederation was not achieved in just one try. Continue your discussions until you get a measure of agreement upon the objectives which you desire to achieve. Then, having that agreement, work out your financial details accordingly so that you can implement the agreement. That course was not followed at the conference because the conference took the course rather of financial bargaining, and it was on financial grounds that the conference fell down. But I wish to point out that the lack of a financial agreement is no bar to an old age annuity or social insurance scheme.
There are figures to support that contention. In the first place, as a result of the fact that two provinces have indicated that they will not sign, and by their not signing, the federal government is being saved-rather, not the federal government but the people of Canada are being saved-approximately $100 million a year; for, according to the figures given by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, that is what it would cost the federal treasury to pay to Ontario and Quebec the grant which was offered in the latest proposals made to them. Second the great tax fields of personal and corporation income tax, which it was regarded as essential that the dominion should use exclusively, are as open now as they would be if all the provinces had signed, because Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia have not reentered these tax fields and therefore they are fully open to the dominion government to be used for the purposes of its own old age pensions scheme or any other

social security scheme which it may envisage. Third, the government of Ontario is pressing and has pressed consistently since the breakdown of the conference on financial matters for a reconvening of the conference to discuss the social security and other measures involved. Actually it is too expensive for us to go on paying grants to seven provinces which have signed, without getting together and implementing a social security scheme, because those grants are costing $100 million a year more now without the social security scheme than the first proposals of the dominion government which included that scheme. This last figure is based on the statement of the Minister of Finance on page 1841 of Hansard.
Having dealt with the subject of dominion-provincial relations in its relationship to this question, I wish to come to the bill actually before the house and to outline what I regard as certain weaknesses in the present old age pension scheme now in effect and to be in effect when this amending bill passes the house. The first great lack is that it does not take any steps toward a contributory old age pension scheme. It is important to keep clear in our minds that the two things are quite separate. What this bill envisages is in no sense a contributory old age pension scheme, but I am sure that if we are to have a proper social security system in this country we must eventually arrive at a contributory old age annuity or insurance scheme. So that the first failure of the bill is that it takes no step in that direction.
Second, the bill continues certain of the unjustifiable restrictions and unjustifiable hardships present in the current old age pension system. It continues certain restrictions as to eligibility which impose tremendous hardships on applicants; particularly, the proof of continuous residence in Canada for twenty years, and the other provisions in that connection. These contain qualifications which it is almost impossible for many applicants for pension to fulfil or prove.
Third, the bill continues certain measures with regard to deductions from pension which will be made if the pensioner has a certain income, so-called, of his own, for instance, the rent calculated from property. This is not actual income received by the pensioner. It is only hypothetical income and is received only in the minds of the government or of the pension authority. If the pensioner owns a home the bill provides that he shall be regarded as if he received an income from it and he will be charged what they figure to be a reasonable rent for that home. This actually penalizes thrift and discourages good citizenship, because the person looking toward the

Old Age Pensions
eventual receipt of a pension will find that he is better off if he parts with his home or does not build one at all. Surely it is not logical or proper to continue a provision which discourages a person from owning his own home.

From a review of the old age statistics available in Canada today, it seems that there is necessity for two things. The first is a scientific study of the whole question of old age and our approach to the problem; the second is a contributory scheme of old age insurance. Statistics show that ninety years ago the average life expectancy of a Canadian was forty years. This has increased until at the present time it is approximately sixty-five years, and information available indicates that in future the

I am giving the figures from the 1941 census. Then I think one realizes the tremendous financial burden it will be to this country to take care of this growing group of older people unless we have a sound approach to this question; and that, in turn, indicates the ultimate necessity of instituting a contributory scheme of old age annuities. I have disagreed somewhat violently with the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), but with one thing he said tonight I agree completely; that is, that the older people of this countiy do not want these old age pensions to be charity. They want to contribute; they want to provide for their own old age, for their own requirements now and in the closing years of their lives.
The statistics I have given indicate further the desperate condition which will prevail if the welfare aspect of this question is not studied. Of the two problems, financial and welfare, perhaps welfare is as important as, if not more important than, the financial problem. If you consider the position of a senior citizen, surely it will be seen that it is bad enough to have the spectre of financial hardship looming, over you when you reach the declining years of your life; but when, in addition, you have uncertainty as to whether your closing years will be of any use to yourself or to anybody else, whether you will be perhaps a trial and a burden to your family or to the state; when you have this spiritual and moral uncertainty, as well as the physical and financial questions looming over you, then the picture for our old people is pretty grim. I believe this emphasizes the need for assurance to these people of adequate housing, food and care; and perhaps most important, the provision of an adequate method by which they may train themselves to make full and proper use of the leisure time available to them and to do all these things without being a burden to any individual, to their family 
or their friends, and without being regarded as a burden on the state. Those who have experience in these fields are aware of, and have frequently emphasized, the independence of spirit of our older people. It seems to me that this is a tremendous asset which we should recognize and on which we should capitalize, so that instead of as at present, if I may use this phrase, the older people of Canada in large measure being a wasting asset, we should regard them as a tremendous potential asset capable of making a real contribution to the community and the country in which they live. If we make provision for them to train themselves not only to look after themselves, but to help the community in which they live, then we shall be rendering, not only to these older people, but to Canada itself, a tremendous service.
It seems that at the present time there are only two or three alternatives open to older citizens in this position. They may go into an institution, one of our old men's homes; they may be a burden upon their family or friends; or they may eke out their last years in loneliness, in single rooms or shacks perhaps as far away as they can get from the companionship of their fellow citizens. This, I am afraid, is where you find most of them. I believe this is partly due to the inadequate financial measures which have already been discussed, but it is perhaps also largely due to a lack of effective interest-and I repeat the words, effective interest-on the part of the country and the community, and a lack of leadership on the part of the dominion government. No effective approach to this problem has ever been made along the lines of helping these people, by training and encouragement, to work out their own arrangements for the closing years of their lives so that they may be lived where they have been accustomed to live, in the company of their families and friends, where they can continue useful work, making a contribution to the community and to the country, instead of being forced to adopt one of the alternatives I have outlined.
In closing this section of my remarks, I wish to draw one parallel, if I may. The problem of juvenile delinquency is recognized, and steps are taken to counter that threat to our national life. But juvenile delinquency is not inevitable. Old age is inevitable, and surely in itself that is an argument in favour of recognizing the problem and taking effective steps to meet it.
In conclusion, then, may I say that I feel there is no reason, merely because we have not yet reached financial agreement between

I should like to be permitted to conclude my speech. Canada has been most generous to some of her citizens. I mentioned that our standard of living was higher during the war than during any previous period in our history. I have here the statistical summary of the Bank of Canada, and on page 48 there will be found a table showing the net income to stockholders in the industrial classification. If you compare the net income received in 1938 with that received in 1945 you will find that in the case of grain mill products their position improved from $0-2 million in the red to $2-6 million in the clear. Those in the food industry improved their position from $8-5 million to $12-2 million. Those in the drink business improved their position from $5-8 million to $12-3 million. The tobacco industry did not fare quite so well, but the pulp and paper industry improved their position from $0-3 million to $15-8 million, and so on down the list. It will be found that industrial concerns in Canada greatly improved their position during the war.
At my request, certain sessional papers were brought down showing just what the government is doing with regard to the payment of pensions in some of the departments. I suggest that the Department of Justice is the department in which citizens of this country should seek to find employment if they wish

to have adequate pensions for their old age. I find that eighty-two pensioners listed by the Department of Justice are getting pensions totalling $372,397, or annual pensions of $4,541. I might point out that these pensions are paid without any means test; there are no questions asked as to whether there are children who are able to provide support, whether you have stocks or bonds and so on. When those eighty-two citizens receive $378 a month without a means test I find it difficult to understand how 200,000 citizens of this country can be expected to get by on $360 for the whole year.
In conclusion, 1 wish to say that Canada has done many things of which we are proud. "Canada from Sea to Sea" states:
Land, climate and people are generally recognized as the chief elements in making of a nation. What the people do with the land and its resources, helped or hindered by climate, makes the country's economic history. How they organize their united strength for freedom and security makes their political history. Social and cultural development can be measured by the extent to which people master their environment and build on the traditions they have inherited.
It also mentions that about thirty per cent of our vast output of raw materials was allocated to our Canadian forces during the war. It says:
Almost overnight Canada was transformed from a producer of food and raw materials into one of the world's major manufacturing nations.
It mentions that Canada leads the world in the output of newsprint, nickel, radium, platinum and asbestos, and ranks second in wood-pulp, aluminum and gold, and that sufficient Canadian wheat is grown annually on Canadian farms to meet the normal bread requirements of 92.000,000 people. It goes on to say:
During the war Canada supplied the United Kingdom with 72 per cent of its bacon, 52 per cent of its wheat, 35 per cent of its canned fish and a quarter of its cheese. Canada stood fourth among the United Nations in total war production.
Let me remind the house that Canada gave of these riches to help feed people who were fighting for our liberty, and all I ask now is that we should give of our surplus so that the elder citizens of this country will not have to look forward to the years ahead with fear and dread, but we should see that they get enough food to eat and enable them to obtain warm clothing, medical services and adequate shelter.

of people whom I know personally who are entitled to old age pensions due to their disabilities or infirmities and who cannot get them because they have not reached the age of seventy or because they are not blind at forty. That is a story which is common knowledge to all. Therefore, sir, one must realize that reform is a very difficult thing. It requires determination, good will and honesty of purpose. It is very difficult indeed and takes a long time to be accomplished.
Of course, if some hon. members agree that a survey should be made, after a selection, an honest selection, a fair selection between the needy cases and the other cases, everybody will realize that it is a hard thing to do. Once more what will be considered will not be the need today but what is to be done to please. That is that. The aim is not to accomplish one's duty; the aim is to please the largest possible number. Well, if it is the definite purpose of the government to please the largest number of people they are bound to make that survey; they, are bound to complete it after a selection, and they have to decide not to pay any longer pensions to those who have received it as a pure gift or a bribe without being entitled to it, and to use that amount to fill the gaps and to help those who are really in need. I hope that is clear enough.
I shall make another suggestion to the minister. It is impossible to pay pensions from the cradle to the grave to all persons in Canada. But in a society, in an organized state, support must come from the state to those who cannot get it otherwise. There should be a campaign of education to teach the people the purpose of old age pensions. It is to help those who cannot get any help otherwise. I will tell you more than that. I said at first, that the contribution to the provinces is necessary because the provinces have no means to pay the old age pensions alone, but the management of old age pensions by the provinces was a mistake, as it should be by the municipalities themselves.
I have been informed that in some western provinces no old age pension is granted unless it is approved beforehand by the municipal council. That is one thing, but I will go one step further. Since the municipal administration is the closest to the people and since the taxpayers have the opportunity to judge if the money is well spent or wrongly spent by the municipality, there should be in each municipality a list of those who receive old age pensions. If such lists were posted at the entrance to the city hall in each municipality, I am sure, that the effect would be magical,

and there are many people who would be ashamed to consider any longer the acceptance of any grant of old1 age pensions.
I do not want anyone to conclude from what I have said that I am opposed to old age pensions; far from it. The thing is now on the statute books and we cannot dispense with it. This is the danger of social legislation. When the people have tasted something like this it is impossible as a rule to deprive them of the whole thing. But the matter can be settled in accordance with the very high principle of justice, fairness and honesty to which I have referred, and the people will appreciate the fact that pensions must be paid only to those who are entitled to them on account of sickness, disability and poverty, lack of support, and the fact that they are alone in the world. When a man or a woman is alone in the world the state must come to his or her help, because he or she is one of us and we cannot abandon them on the road.
These are a few considerations that I have wanted to make for a very long time. It is high time to come to our senses and not to practise "electoralism" with matters such as old age pensions. What is "electoralism"? It is spending the people's funds without a useful purpose and just to please or appease a certain category of people. At the present time we are pleasing the old; it is all right; I have respect for the old. My best friends were very old people who were very kind to me and whom I shall never forget. I have respect for the old; I am ready to assist the old, but I think it would be an insult to offer crutches to an old gentleman who is able to walk and that is why, sir, I shall not insist any longer on it. I think I have made my position clear. I sincerely believe that if an independent and honest survey were made of the whole question of old age pensions one would realize that in many of the cases these pensions are a waste of money because they are given to people who do not need them. I believe it is absolutely absurd to put all the old people in the same category. It is unfair to them, and if it is accepted by them it shows how low our population has fallen, but I do not believe it. If hon. gentlemen who are not convinced of what I have said received the complaints, the just- and fair complaints, that I receive from people who will not be allowed to receive anything under this scheme and who deserves it more than the old Croesuses who get it they would change their mind immediately. It is not because I have a heart of stone that I have spoken as I have done.

I thank my hon. friend very much, and I can pay the same compliment to him for whom I have the deepest admiration.
We have reached the time when we cannot bribe the old by giving old age pensions that they are not entitled to get while others deserve pensions that they cannot get. There should be an adjustment, not on a basis of age, but on a basis of need, and that is what I wanted to say. I thank the house very warmly for the kind reception that was given to me when I made these remarks, and I hope again that the hon. gentlemen who have listened to me so closely will think about what I have said. If they do, they will realize that I was not in the wrong when I came down to brass tacks to improve the old age pensions scheme.

I will now give my ruling on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and on the point of order raised by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). The amendment moved by Mr. Blackmore reads:
That Bill No 339 be not now read the second time, but that the same be referred back to the government for their earnest consideration of the following provisions:
(a)	Reduction of the pensionable age to not more than 65 years.
(b)	Increase in the general pension to not less than $50 a month.
(c)	Complete abolition of the means test.
I would direct the attention of the house to the language of the motion, that the bill be not now read the second time but that the same be referred back to the government for their earnest consideration. An amendment to refer a bill back to the government is an expanded negative, if you consider that the government is the sponsor of the bill. The house may, after second reading, decide that the bill be referred to the committee of the whole and it may, in certain circumstances, refer it to a select committee, but there is no precedent of a bill having been referred to the government, which in the present case is not only the sponsor ol the bill, but moreover is not a parliamentary agency. Hon. members know that when a bill has been introduced in the house the bill becomes the property of the house. It is the privilege of the house to refer a bill to the committee of the whole, to a standing committee, to any agency of parliament; but it is out of order since the bill is the property of parliament, to refer it to an agency which is not a part of parliament. The amendment offends all principles of parliamentary procedure and cannot be moved. I would go farther. In my humble opinion, if it were the privilege of members of the house to
move that a bill be referred to the government, it would be also the privilege of any member to refer a bill to one of the parties sitting in this house. If a bill could be referred to the government, I think it could be referred to the Progressive Conservative party or to the C.C.F. or to the Social Credit party. I have therefore no hesitation in declaring the amendment out of order.
